## Calibration prompt — the claim to contest

*Commit before you read anything. Thirty seconds.*

**The claim:** *"Your report template was designed to record what you found, not to survive someone
attacking it."*

**Is that true of your template?** *True of us* or *not true of us*, and the one sentence you would
defend it with.

**And the number you will check.** Lesson 1 sets out **six elements** a finder of fact looks for in an
investigation report. **How many of the six does your current template actually require**, not
permit, require, such that leaving it out would look like an omission?

Out of six. Commit before you see the list.

## Module brief

This is the most frequent thing you write and the thing most likely to be read years later by
somebody whose job is to undermine it.

**A note on why this module exists here, since another track covers adjacent ground.** The HR business
partner track teaches a generalist how to use AI on ER documents safely: structure, language
discipline, a completeness check, and a provenance rule. That is the right content for somebody who
writes an investigation summary twice a year, and this track's learners will never see it, because a
learner sees exactly one 301 track.

**So this module teaches the specialist version, and it is a different subject.** Not *how to use AI on
a document* but **what the document has to do**, and therefore what AI may touch in each part of it.
The generalist question is about safety. Yours is about function: this report is an instrument with a
job, and every rule below follows from the job rather than from caution.

Four things: what the report is structurally for, the completeness question that is specific to
investigations, how to hold the ladder's rungs at the level of a sentence, and (new since this track
was outlined) **what putting investigation material into an AI tool may do to privilege**, which now
has case law on both sides of it.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module you should be able to:

1. Name the six elements a finder of fact looks for, and explain why elements make a report's gaps
   visible where narrative hides them.
2. Run the investigation-specific completeness pass: **which allegation did I fail to resolve?**
3. Detect a rung breach at sentence level: an inference or determination wearing an observation's
   grammar.
4. Describe the provenance discipline and why the chain matters more than any single sentence.
5. State what two 2026 rulings suggest about AI tools and privilege `[V]`, and what the practical
   consequence is.

## Lesson 1 · The report has legal work to do

Start with function, because structure follows from it and most templates have inherited a structure
that follows from nothing.

An investigation report is read by people asking specific questions. A decision-maker deciding what
to do. An appeal panel deciding whether the process was sound. Eventually, possibly, a tribunal or a
court deciding whether the employer acted reasonably. Every one of them is looking for the same
things, and there are six:

1. **What was alleged**: each allegation identified separately, in the complainant's terms.
2. **What was investigated**: the scope, and **what was excluded and why.**
3. **What evidence was gathered, and from whom** — including what was sought and not obtained.
4. **What could not be established, and why**: the deliberate record of the gaps.
5. **What was found**: allegation by allegation, mapping back to element 1.
6. **On what standard** — named, and applied visibly.

Now the structural claim this lesson turns on:

> **A report organized as a narrative is a report whose gaps are invisible. A report organized as
> elements makes its own gaps visible to you first.**

A narrative report reads chronologically and persuasively, and a gap in a narrative looks like a
transition. *"Following the meeting, the complainant raised further concerns…"*, did you investigate
the meeting? A reader cannot tell, and neither can you when you re-read your own draft, because the
prose is doing what prose does and carrying the reader past the joint.

An elements report cannot hide the same gap. Allegation three has no findings paragraph. The gap is a
blank space with a heading over it, and **you** are the first person to see it rather than the last.

Which is also where AI's permission enters, because the structure determines it. Elements 1 to 4 are
rungs one and two: what was alleged, what was looked at, what exists, what does not. **AI is
permitted and useful across all four.** Elements 5 and 6 are rungs four and five. Nothing.

**One honest caveat**, because the elements structure is not free: it is a worse read. Lesson 1's
structure serves the person auditing your process. A decision-maker who has to act may need a
narrative summary as well, and the answer is both — a short narrative up front, and the elements
underneath it, with the narrative explicitly labelled as a summary of the elements rather than the
findings themselves. The *Take a position* section is about whether that compromise holds.

## Lesson 2 · The completeness pass, specialized

The generalist version of the completeness question is *what did I fail to ask?* It is a good question
and it is not the one that catches the defect that ends investigations.

**The specialist version is:**

> **Which allegation did I fail to resolve?**

Here is the failure it catches, and it is the most common serious defect in investigation reports. A
complainant raises four things. Three are substantial, one is vague or awkward or arrived in a final
paragraph. The investigation addresses the three. The report makes findings on the three. **The fourth
is never mentioned again**, not rejected, not found unsubstantiated, not recorded as outside scope.
It simply disappears.

Why this specific defect matters more than most:

- **It is mechanical to detect.** Anybody comparing the intake to the findings finds it in five
  minutes, which means opposing counsel finds it first and free.
- **It is unanswerable.** You cannot explain at a hearing why allegation four was not addressed if
  nobody made a decision about it, because there is no decision to describe.
- **It is often the allegation that mattered.** The vague one is frequently the one about a protected
  characteristic, or the retaliation complaint, which arrives last and least clearly precisely because
  it is the hardest to say.

**And it is a genuinely good use of AI**, which is the point of putting it here. This is a **coverage
audit against a list**: allegations in, findings out, flag the mismatches. It evaluates nobody. It
makes no judgment about merit. It is rung two, it is fully permitted, and it is exactly the sort of
mechanical completeness check where a model does not get bored at item four.

The operational form:

- Extract the allegations from the intake **as a numbered list**, before the investigation starts.
  Module 1's structured intake exists for this.
- At draft stage, ask for a mapping: **each allegation, and the section of the report that resolves
  it.** Unmapped allegations listed explicitly.
- **A resolution includes "outside scope" and "insufficient evidence to determine."** Those are
  findings. Silence is not.
- Run it against the **complainant's own framing**, not your restatement, restating an allegation more
  narrowly and then resolving the narrower version is the same defect wearing a suit.

## Lesson 3 · The rung boundary, sentence by sentence

Module 1 gave you the ladder. This is the ladder applied to prose, which is where it either works or
turns out to have been a diagram.

Three sentences about the same moment:

- *"Raised his voice twice, according to two witnesses."* — **Observation.** Attributed, quantified,
  sourced.
- *"Was hostile during the meeting."* — **Finding**, wearing an observation's grammar. "Hostile" is a
  characterization of a person, and no witness said it; you concluded it.
- *"Intended to intimidate the complainant."* — **Determination**, smuggled into a clause. A finding
  about state of mind, presented as description.

All three are the same length and the same tense. The second and third are the ones that end
investigations, and they are not lies. They may be entirely correct conclusions. **The problem is
that the sentence gives the reader no way to tell which rung produced it**, which means at a hearing
you will be asked to justify a conclusion you may not remember reaching.

**Now the legitimate AI use here, and it is the only place in this track where a model may edit your
language.** A model is unusually good at flagging where a sentence's register has slipped, where a
characterization has appeared in a section that should contain observations, where an adjective is
doing the work of a finding.

The permission, stated exactly:

> **A model may tell you that a sentence has climbed a rung. It may never tell you which rung is
> right.**

The first is a linguistic audit (*this sentence contains a characterization*) and it is checkable in
seconds by looking at the sentence. The second is the finding, and it is yours.

So the prompt shape that stays inside the line: *"Identify sentences containing characterizations,
conclusions about state of mind, or evaluative adjectives, and quote them."* Not: *"rewrite these
neutrally"*, which hands the model the choice of what the neutral version asserts, and not *"is this
conclusion supported?"*, which is rung four.

Three specific patterns worth searching your own drafts for:

- **Evaluative adjectives in factual sections.** Hostile, aggressive, unprofessional, dismissive,
  evasive. Each is a conclusion.
- **State-of-mind verbs.** Intended, attempted, knew, deliberately. You almost never have evidence of
  these directly; you have conduct from which you inferred them, and the inference belongs on its own
  rung.
- **Unattributed passive constructions.** *"It was felt that…"*, *"concerns were raised…"* Who felt,
  who raised. An unattributed conclusion is a conclusion whose author cannot be examined, which is the
  opposite of what this document is for.

## Lesson 4 · Provenance and privilege [V]

Two properties of the finished document, and the second one has changed since this track was planned.

### Provenance: the chain, not the sentence

The questions asked under oath are always the same four: **who wrote this, when, based on what, and
did it change?** A document whose production you cannot describe is weaker than one you can, and that
was true before any of this existed.

Four practices, and note that only one is about AI:

- **Keep contemporaneous notes separately from the report**, and do not overwrite them. The note is
  evidence of what you knew when.
- **Preserve the file's chronology.** When a finding was reached matters as much as what it was.
- **Record AI involvement as one line in your file notes**: what it did, at which stage, on what date.
  Not as a disclaimer on the report; as a fact in the record.
- **And the rule that governs the rest:** a model's phrasing must never become a finding you did not
  independently reach. If a sentence in your final document is one whose origin you could not describe
  under questioning, rewrite it in your own words or delete it.

### Privilege: two 2026 rulings, opposite outcomes **[V]**

Whether your investigation is privileged is a question for counsel and depends on how it was set up.
What is new (and what makes this a lesson rather than a caution) is that courts have begun to
address what **using an AI tool** does to that protection, and the two most instructive rulings point
in opposite directions.

**In February 2026**, a federal district judge in the Southern District of New York held that material
generated through a **consumer AI tool** at a criminal defendant's own prompting was **not** protected
by attorney-client privilege or the work-product doctrine. Two strands of reasoning matter to you.
First, **third-party waiver**: inputting privileged information into the tool was treated as sharing it
with a third party, which may waive privilege over the underlying communications. Second, the *Kovel*
doctrine (which can extend privilege to a third party whose assistance counsel needs) did not apply,
because the tool was not necessary for counsel to understand the client, and because **the defendant
engaged it on his own initiative rather than at counsel's direction.**

**And in May 2026**, in the *Mobley v. Workday* litigation, a magistrate judge **denied** a motion to
compel production of a vendor's AI bias-testing data, finding it privileged **because the vendor's
attorneys had curated the analysis and used its results in providing legal advice.**

Read together:

> **Two 2026 rulings, opposite outcomes, and the variable that separated them was whether counsel
> directed the work.**

Which is the same principle this curriculum states elsewhere in a different context: **structure
determines protection.** The analysis is the same either way; the discovery consequence is not.

**Carry the caveats, because the argument rests on them.** The February ruling is a district-court decision
in a criminal matter involving a consumer tool. **It is not a holding about workplace investigations**,
and nobody should tell you the law is settled. What commentators identify as the likely factors,
whether the platform is open or closed, whether contractual or policy confidentiality protections
exist, and whether counsel directed or supervised the use — are a description of where courts appear
to be looking, not a test you can rely on.

**The practical consequence is nonetheless clear enough to act on**, and it is cheap:

- **If an investigation may be privileged, the AI question belongs in the engagement, not afterwards.**
  Counsel decides whether a tool is used, which tool, and for what, before the work starts.
- **The platform matters.** A consumer account and an enterprise deployment with confidentiality terms
  are different facts, and Lesson 4's third-party-waiver reasoning is why.
- **And the ten-minute conversation is now.** Asking counsel *may we use this tool on privileged
  investigation material, and under what conditions* is a question with an answer. Asking after
  somebody has requested your file is not a conversation, it is a disclosure.

### Try this — 3 minutes
Open your report template) the actual document, not your memory of it. Count how many of Lesson
1's six elements it *requires*. Then find the section where a finding would go if nobody had thought
about allegation four, and check whether the template would notice.

## Key takeaways

- **Six elements a finder of fact looks for:** what was alleged, what was investigated (and what was
  excluded and why), what evidence was gathered and from whom, **what could not be established and
  why**, what was found allegation by allegation, and on what standard.
- **A narrative report's gaps look like transitions. An elements report's gaps are blank spaces with
  headings over them**, and you see them first rather than last. Elements 1–4 are rungs one and two,
  where AI is permitted and useful; elements 5 and 6 are rungs four and five, where it is not.
- **The completeness question is "which allegation did I fail to resolve?"**, not "what did I fail to
  ask." The unaddressed fourth allegation is mechanical to detect, unanswerable at a hearing, and
  frequently the one that mattered.
- **A resolution includes "outside scope" and "insufficient evidence." Silence is not a resolution** —
  and run the check against the **complainant's own framing**, because restating an allegation more
  narrowly and resolving the narrower version is the same defect in a suit.
- **Three sentence-level rung breaches:** evaluative adjectives in factual sections (hostile,
  evasive), state-of-mind verbs (intended, knew), and unattributed passives (*"it was felt that"*).
- **A model may tell you a sentence has climbed a rung. It may never tell you which rung is right.**
  This is the only place in the track where a model may touch your language, and the reason is that it
  is auditing register rather than reaching a conclusion.
- **Provenance is about the chain:** who wrote it, when, based on what, and did it change. Keep notes
  separately, preserve the chronology, record AI involvement as a line in the file, and **never let a
  model's phrasing become a finding you did not independently reach.**
- **Two 2026 rulings on AI and privilege point opposite ways, and the variable was whether counsel
  directed the work** `[V]`. Third-party waiver reasoning applied to a consumer tool used on a party's
  own initiative; privilege upheld where attorneys curated the analysis for legal advice. **Neither is
  a workplace-investigation holding.** The practical move is the same either way: **if it may be
  privileged, the AI question belongs in the engagement.**

## Take a position

**The claim:** *"A report organized as a narrative is a report whose gaps are invisible."*

The strongest counter-argument is that **an elements report is unreadable by the people who most need
to act on it, and an unread report is worse than a slightly gappy one.**

Narrative is how people understand events. A decision-maker choosing a sanction, a manager
implementing an outcome, an appeal panel reviewing fairness: all of them need to know **what
happened**, in order, with causation visible. An elements report gives them a compliance artifact and
asks them to assemble the story themselves, which they will do badly and in their heads, where you
cannot see the version they built.

And investigations do not arrive in elements. They arrive as sequences, and some of the most important
findings are **narrative findings**: that the conduct escalated after a specific event, that a pattern
emerged only once a third party was involved, that the complainant's account changed after they were
told something. Forcing that into a schema can obscure the very structure that constitutes the
finding.

There is a professional version of the objection too, and it is uncomfortable. **The best investigators
write well and persuasively.** An elements template is a floor for weak investigators, and floors have
a way of becoming ceilings, a form that guarantees adequacy also discourages the well-argued report
that explains why the evidence points where it does.

Your position has to say whether the elements structure is a **floor or a form** — whether you would
accept a well-argued narrative report from an experienced investigator, and if so, **what you would
check instead** to catch the unaddressed fourth allegation. Because that defect is the one the
structure exists to prevent, and if you allow narrative you need another mechanism for it. Note that
this module already proposes one: the mapping check in Lesson 2 works on any structure.

## Sources and attribution

- **Privilege and AI tools, 2026** `[V]`. A February 2026 ruling by a federal district judge in the
  Southern District of New York held that material generated through a **consumer AI tool** at a
  criminal defendant's own prompting was not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product,
  reasoning that inputting privileged information into the tool was sharing with a third party, and
  that the *Kovel* doctrine did not apply because the tool was not necessary for counsel's
  understanding and was engaged on the party's own initiative rather than at counsel's direction. And a
  May 2026 magistrate ruling in ***Mobley v. Workday*** denied a motion to compel a vendor's AI
  bias-testing data on privilege grounds **because counsel curated the analysis and used its results in
  providing legal advice.** Commentators identify the likely factors as the open or closed nature of
  the platform, the existence of contractual or policy confidentiality protections, and whether counsel
  directed or supervised the use. **Neither ruling is a holding about workplace investigations. This is
  a description of where courts appear to be looking, not a test to rely on, and it should be checked
  with counsel before it changes practice.** The *Mobley* phrasing is aligned with
  `ai301-peopleops-m7`, which cites the same ruling, so the two do not drift. **[V]**
- The six elements, the narrative-hides-gaps argument, the
  **which-allegation-did-I-fail-to-resolve** pass, the three sentence-level rung breaches, the
  flag-but-never-choose permission, and the four provenance practices are original to this course.
- Builds on Module 1 of this track (the evidentiary ladder, applied here to prose, which is where it
  either works or turns out to be a diagram) and Module 3 (the record this document is built from).
- **On its relationship to `ai301-hrbp-m6`.** That module teaches a generalist to use AI on ER
  documents safely (structure, language discipline, a completeness pass, and a provenance rule) and
  a learner sees exactly one 301 track, so the overlap costs nobody anything. **This is the specialist
  version and a different subject:** not how to use AI on a document but what the document has to do.
  Recorded so the two remain reconcilable rather than drifting into contradiction.
